rewrites.blindSummary:
The country demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: a local observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022 — hundreds of incidents and dozens of deaths — with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. The country's officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds they are not “biological women.” There is no legal gender recognition and no SOGI hate-crime statute (a 2022 law actually increased penalties for “aggravated” LGBT visibility before being struck down).

The national legislature has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives (a 2022 bill, later shelved after protests). The community is organised (a local group, plus trans collectives) but under pressure. Tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from the general violence level.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is documented and dangerous: a human-rights organisation (7 October 2020) records that the country's authorities facilitate anti-trans violence by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence including sexual assault — a trans activist described being forced into sex at night while held in a men's prison. Placement operated by birth sex in the men's prison system as of 2020, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, no special trans unit, and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice on record; in a country with no legal gender recognition, a detained trans visitor faces men's prison placement with documented sexual-assault risk and no documented custody rule or court ruling anchoring a remedy.
rewrites.blindTangential:
A regional human-rights court's 2017 advisory opinion advanced gender recognition in four regional countries, including this one, with compliance still uncertain; a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four.

Legislative flux: early-2022 bills sought to erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition, and anti-trans initiatives have repeatedly advanced in the national legislature.

The custody finding sits inside a regional and asylum frame: the human-rights report documenting birth-sex prison placement is the chapter of a three-country report that also examines obstacles to asylum elsewhere; it documents no trans-specific custody policy or court ruling for this country, and the same report records that a local LGBTQ organisation flags forced internal displacement from violence generally — refugee/context material, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The femicide-law exclusion of trans women and the absence of legal gender recognition are resident-facing; the documented violence toll — 147 recorded cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders in 2022 (hundreds of incidents, dozens of deaths) — falls on residents.

The organised community (a local group and trans collectives) operates under pressure from the repeated legislative attacks.

Resident custody: the documented practice of placing trans women in men's prisons by birth sex, with sexual-assault exposure (a trans activist's account), governs residents held in the system, and a local LGBTQ organisation flags forced internal displacement of LGBTI people from violence generally — a resident burden; a visitor meets the custody practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved: how the general violence level in communities outside the tourist areas applies to visitors is unquantified — general gang violence affects all travellers, and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners but not insulated from it.

Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources, and the femicide-law exclusion is resident-facing though it signals institutional stance.

Prison axis: the birth-sex placement finding rests on a single human-rights organisation's documentation (7 October 2020); no law, regulation, court ruling or custody policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented — in a country without legal gender recognition, that absence cannot be read as a protected standard.
blindSourceSummaries: An encyclopedic article on killings of trans women records that governments in the region have long excluded trans women from femicide protections, with officials justifying the exclusion on the grounds that transgender women are not 'biological women'.

A May 2024 foundation report: a regional human-rights court's 2017 gender-identity opinion advanced legal gender recognition in four regional countries, but a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four.
A January 2022 human-rights group news piece documents legislative attacks on trans people, including bills that would erase gender identity protections and restrict legal recognition.
A January 2018 news report: countries including this one urged to abide by a regional human-rights court ruling requiring marriage equality and gender recognition — compliance status uncertain.

A 7 October 2020 human-rights report chapter: authorities facilitate anti-trans violence by placing trans women in men's prisons, exposing them to violence including sexual assault; a trans activist described being sexually assaulted at night while held in a men's prison; it documents birth-sex placement in the men's prison system as of 2020, with no gender-identity-based placement policy, special trans unit, or trans-specific solitary/segregation practice, and records a local LGBTQ organisation flagging forced internal displacement from violence generally.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is broadly workable for trans visitors — there is no criminalisation, courts have protected trans people's restroom access and ruled favourably on legal gender recognition, and the capital hosts one of the region's largest Pride parades. There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner, and no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering services. No severe incidents involving trans visitors are documented. The capital's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are welcoming; outside them, more caution is warranted.

The consequence axis of an arrest is largely undocumented: no source in this record describes how transgender prisoners are housed in the country's civilian prison system — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice — and no civilian trans-prisoner case surfaced. The one documented trans placement case inside the country's custody system is military rather than civilian: a transgender conscript was compulsorily discharged in early 2020 after a military panel classified the effects of her gender-affirming surgery as a physical/mental handicap; she died by suicide in March 2021; a district court ruled the discharge unjust and reinstated her posthumously on 7 October 2021; and in March 2024 the defence ministry recognised her death as in the line of duty — a harsh institutional default corrected by the courts only after death. For a detained trans visitor, civilian prison placement is simply unknown: in a legal system where legal gender recognition is possible and courts have repeatedly ruled for trans people, recourse would likely exist, but the placement practice itself is unverified — not a verified midpoint and not verified safe.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Compared with its closest comparable peers, the legal baseline has documented gaps: no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and no same-sex marriage. Policy and litigation flux: a December 2024 martial-law crisis and related assembly-freedom questions, a 2024 constitutional ruling recognising same-sex partners' healthcare rights, and organised conservative opposition set a moving political backdrop rather than direct street-level risk.

Custody-axis framing: the only trans placement case inside the country's custody system on record is a military conscript case — a conscript's discharge, death, posthumous reinstatement and line-of-duty recognition — rather than a civilian prison case; the criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel (the military criminal code, article 92-6, up to two years' imprisonment) and the exclusion of transgender people from military service are resident-conscript-facing, not visitor-facing.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The court-based legal gender recognition process (surgery was historically required but courts are moving to allow changes without it), the hospital-ward 'transgender blind spot' (the health ministry cannot answer how to accommodate trans patients), school-bathroom friction, and the military-service harassment data (12% of trans people assigned male at birth who served in the mandatory military experienced sexual harassment or violence — this affects conscripts, not foreign visitors) are all resident-facing.

Further resident data: 67% of trans youth report hearing transphobic remarks from teachers; same-sex conduct is criminalised in the military under the military criminal code (upheld in 2023); and a nationwide survey documents a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

The one documented institutional case is a conscript's: the individual stood under mandatory military service and the military criminal code — legal machinery that does not reach visitors; transgender people are excluded from military service, and the military same-sex-conduct ban governs serving personnel, while nothing is documented about how trans people are housed in the civilian prison system at all.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Foreign-tourist taxi scams and shopping complaints rose 71% in 2024 — general, not trans-specific.

One source — a supreme-court family-register decision — could not be retrieved at research time, so that ruling's detail rests on its summary. No border-screening or document-handling practice specific to trans visitors is documented in this record.

Prison axis: no rule, regulation, case or practice is documented on civilian trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no special unit, no solitary/segregation practice; the only placement case on record is the military discharge case (an administrative discharge, not a prison-housing case). Where a detained trans visitor would be housed in the civilian system is unverified, and that gap cannot be read as evidence of either identity-based placement or mistreatment.
blindSourceSummaries: A July 2024 court judgment, final with no appeal: police advising a trans person undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, with symbolic compensation awarded for the infringement.

A May 2024 court ruling: a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery to change legal sex status — five plaintiffs assigned male at birth and on hormone therapy for years; the court held that demanding surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals.
A March 2024 research report: trans teens avoid school restrooms for fear of being outed; researchers urged law and institutional reforms for safer school environments.

A November 2023 report: the national human-rights watchdog flagged a 'transgender blind spot in hospitalisation' — the health ministry rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, saying accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

A country overview (updated March 2026): civilian same-sex conduct legal but criminalised in the military under the military criminal code, upheld in 2023; legal gender recognition possible; no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

A peer-reviewed nationwide survey (June 2025): hundreds of transgender and non-binary young adults mapped milestones and stigmatisation across life stages, documenting a pervasive discrimination burden at school, work and in transition-related care.

A 2025 annual report chapter: a relatively positive record with free media and civil society but persistent documented discrimination, also covering a December 2024 martial-law crisis and assembly freedoms.

A travel guide (July 2026): broadly positive for visitors to the capital's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods but requiring contextual understanding — military-law criminalisation, organised conservative opposition, no national anti-discrimination law, alongside rapid social change and a 2024 constitutional ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights.

A source not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying entry covers a supreme-court decision allowing a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register.

An encyclopedic overview: no dedicated coverage of trans prisoners; documents the only prominent trans placement case, military rather than civilian — a conscript discharged in early 2020, death by suicide in March 2021, posthumous reinstatement by a district court on 7 October 2021, and line-of-duty recognition in March 2024; consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel is criminalised (article 92-6, up to two years' imprisonment); transgender people are excluded from military service; no information on civilian trans-prisoner housing — no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country pairs meaningful legal progress with one of the world's highest tolls of violence against transgender people. Of its 32 state/province, 22 offer administrative legal gender recognition; the capital and one other state/province have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections exist. Against that, 71 trans or gender-diverse people were murdered in a single recent year — the second-highest figure in the region — with organised crime increasingly involved and impunity near-total. The victims are overwhelmingly local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit, not tourists; violence is also highly concentrated by region.

In major tourist destinations and the heavily policed, progressively governed capital, a trans visitor's everyday risk is closer to harassment than violence. The dominant hazard for any traveller is the country's general crime environment; state/province-level scores range from among the region's best to levels comparable with its most dangerous regions.

The consequence axis if a trans visitor is arrested is undocumented: the only prison-axis finding in this record — a survey of LGBTQ people in prison — contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement in the country (no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation practice); its sole country-specific item is a July 2007 policy in the capital, adopted through the human-rights commission, allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation. In a nation where legal gender recognition is decided separately in each state/province and official discrimination and near-total impunity for anti-trans violence are documented, where a detained trans visitor would be housed is unverifiable and cannot be assumed to follow identity.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Marriage equality nationwide — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.

Custody-policy context: the sole country-specific prison finding in this record — the capital's July 2007 same-sex conjugal-visit policy stemming from a 2003 anti-discrimination law, applying to all the capital's prisons, with visitors not required to be married to the inmate — is a local custody-conditions measure, not a placement rule; it shows local recognition of sexual-orientation rights inside one city's prisons without any documented counterpart for trans-prisoner placement anywhere in the country.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The administrative legal gender recognition regime, which varies by state/province, and the transfemicide statutes (in the capital and one other state/province) are resident-facing; the 71-murder toll falls overwhelmingly on local trans women (often sex workers and activists) and migrants in transit.

Resident custody: the documented prison-axis finding — the 2007 same-sex conjugal-visit policy in the capital, applying to all its prisons — governs inmates; the undocumented trans-prisoner placement practice (no birth-sex vs identity rule, no trans special units, no solitary/segregation data in any source in this record) concerns residents held in the system; a visitor meets either only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Organised-crime violence, kidnapping, and theft drive several governments to advise caution or non-essential travel avoidance for parts of the country — a risk independent of any personal characteristic.

Prison axis: the single prison-axis source is thin for this country — it documents no birth-sex vs identity placement rule, no trans special units and no solitary/segregation practice, and its only country-specific item (the 2007 policy in the capital on same-sex conjugal visits) says nothing about where trans prisoners are housed; whether a detained trans visitor would be held by the national authorities or by a state/province, and how documents would interact with placement, are unverified in these sources.
blindSourceSummaries: A March 2025 human-rights dispatch: calls on the country's state/province to guarantee administrative legal gender recognition — many now have such procedures, but without recognition, document requests expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation; implementation gaps persist.

A March 2024 human-rights report: barriers to legal name/gender recognition leave trans people exposed — document mismatch amplifies daily discrimination, set against murders including a trans woman found in a river in August 2023.

A July 2024 news report: the capital's legislature approved a law criminalising transfemicide — a watershed named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists say the law is critical for feeling safe.

A January 2024 news report: a wave of transgender killings spurs protests — at least three transgender people killed in early 2024, including an activist shot in the capital, drawing outrage and street protests.

A 2024 regional body press release: urges national and state/province authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanding investigation of all violations with gender-identity-respecting methods; warns impunity may reach alarming levels.

A 2024 analysis: progressive legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly — rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; the authors caution that earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people are safe from violence including murder.

A foreign government travel-advice page: exercise a high degree of caution nationwide due to high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with regional avoid-non-essential-travel advisories in some coastal areas.

A 2024 report: the capital's legislature approved the transfemicide law; regional monitoring records hundreds of transfemicides from 2008 to 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023 — second only to a neighbouring country's figure.

An encyclopedic survey of LGBTQ people in prison, country section: records only one country-specific policy — a July 2007 policy in the capital, adopted through the human-rights commission, allowing same-sex conjugal visits on the basis of a 2003 law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation — and no data on trans-prisoner housing placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. Its legal framework is among the strongest in the region — it ranks 7th on a regional equality ranking, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024, the first to do so in its region. There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people; a regional human-rights court case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show local people markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the regional average (63% avoid holding hands); and a foreign government's travel advisory office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for the country. Major tourist destinations are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

The consequence axis of an arrest is a documented default-plus-petition system: placement of trans women detainees started from the registered sex — the four trans women transferred to a major women's facility on 4 December 2021 had previously been held at two other facilities, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender — and a decision of that date by the senior crime-prevention official created an on-request transfer route to women's facilities, the first documented transfers of trans prisoners to a women's facility in the country. No special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement are documented. A detained trans visitor therefore meets a registered-sex default with an on-request transfer route that demonstrably exists but runs through administrative petition — a workable-but-request-dependent outcome consistent with the country's law-versus-practice gap.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Same-sex marriage legal since 2024 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners; the travel advisory office's LGBTQ warning is a general queer-traveller signal.

Custody-policy context: the 4 December 2021 transfer route was an administrative decision of the senior crime-prevention official (the transfers of the four women — three local nationals and one foreign national — followed each woman's petition), not legislation; an encyclopedic overview of the country's LGBTQ rights confirms that placement starts from the registered sex, with the on-request transfer route for trans women — correctional-administration machinery, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
Resident-facing climate data from the sources: a regional survey (2024) records local residents' avoidance and discrimination burden — 63% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (regional average 53%), 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault, only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ, and 28% felt discriminated against at work; the mob assault on two trans people and the documented police stops and mistreatment of transgender sex workers (the regional human-rights court case) fell on residents.

The documented custody practice is resident-facing: the registered-sex placement default and the 4 December 2021 on-request transfer route govern prisoners held in the local system — the documented transferees were a foreign national and three local nationals held at two other facilities; a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
No trans-specific travel advisory beyond the travel advisory office's general LGBTQ note; ordinary tourist-season crime affects all travellers.

Prison axis: how the on-request transfer route operates in practice — processing time, success rates, conditions before a transfer, and its application to a foreign visitor detained while travelling — is not documented; no trans special units and no rule covering trans men's placement appear in any source, the four December 2021 transfers are the only documented case series, and the sources agree that default placement had followed the male facilities until that decision.
blindSourceSummaries: A 2025 annual regional review (covering 2024): marriage-equality law added equal-treatment guarantees in goods and services, education, healthcare and housing; in March a mob of about 150 attacked two trans people with arrests following; the country's main religious authority officially opposed marriage equality.

A regional human-rights court application (judgment 2017): police stopped and mistreated transgender sex workers and their lawyer in the capital in 2013, with complaints against officers discontinued — documented police conduct toward visibly trans people.

An April 2024 news report: a foreign government's travel advisory office updated its guidance for LGBTQ holidaymakers — same-sex relations legal, civil unions since 2015, marriage since February 2024, legal gender change possible; travellers advised to remain alert.

A 2024 regional survey country sheet: 63% avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner (regional average 53%); 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault; only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ; 28% felt discriminated against at work.

A country profile (updated March 2026): ranked 7th in the region on a 2025 equality ranking; conversion practices banned for minors and intersex infant surgery criminalised in 2022; employment-discrimination ban in 2023; a 2024 marriage-equality law extended equal-treatment grounds across social protection, education, healthcare, housing and goods and services.

A December 2021 news report: four trans detainees were ordered transferred to the women's facilities by decision of the senior crime-prevention official, after each had petitioned for transfer stating they identify and wish to be treated as women; the four — three local nationals and one foreign national — had been held at two other facilities, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender; the first documented transfers of trans prisoners to a women's facility in the country, illustrating that default placement had followed the male facilities and that an on-request transfer route existed.

An encyclopedic overview: same-sex marriage legal since 2024; adoption and foster care; discrimination and hate-speech protections; self-identification gender recognition since 2017; conversion therapy; social conditions including Pride events and homophobic violence; under correctional facilities it confirms placement starts from the registered sex, with an on-request transfer route for trans women.

A May 2025 report: a regional trans-rights index shows backsliding outpacing progress across the region for the first time; the country meets 21 of 32 indicators — gaps include age restrictions on name changes, no national action plan, and no legal recognition of trans parenthood.

rewrites.blindSummary:
The country is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the national prohibition law (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 state/province apply religious law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender social-media personality known by a stage name was found beaten and dead on a highway; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one had been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for “looking gay” — the prohibition law has been described as a “weaponised” law — and dating-app gangs use apps to lure victims into assault and robbery. A foreign government's travel advisory office has warned LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the prohibition law targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the religious-law death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the foreign advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through the country's only recorded trans-imprisonment case: the country's most prominent transgender woman pleaded guilty to four counts of currency abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, and served the term in a maximum-security facility, released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage openly asked which facility she would be kept in, and the report does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section — placement was discretionary — while an October 2024 investigative panel found the maximum-security placement itself unlawful for a first-time offender under the national correctional-service statute. For a trans visitor, the 14-year exposure already applies to tourists; on top of that, detention would land in a prison system with a documented discretionary, unlawfully-assigned placement practice and no recorded housing standard for trans prisoners.
rewrites.blindTangential:
The national prohibition law (14 years, applies to tourists) and the religious-law death penalty in 12 state/province are direct risks for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app luring gangs are a direct app-user risk.

Custody-litigation context: the only trans-prisoner “ruling” on record is the October 2024 investigative panel finding that the celebrity's maximum-security placement violated the national correctional-service statute because she was a first-time offender; the same panel dismissed the bribery allegations that had prompted it — an administrative outcome in a celebrity case, not a rule fixing trans-prisoner housing anywhere in the country.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The documented violence and impunity fall on residents: the killing of the transgender social-media personality with no arrests six months on, police beatings and bribe-extortion of people perceived as gay, the attacks and lost job prospects documented a decade into the prohibition law, and the law's documented reach beyond marriage — cohabitation, any public show of same-sex amorous relationship, and gay organisations criminalised with 10-14 years' prison, with police torture and arbitrary arrests under it (as documented in the 2016 human-rights report).

The recorded imprisonment case is a resident case: the public figure served her sentence in a national prison, and the discretionary placement practice (male or female section left unrecorded, the maximum-security assignment found unlawful for a first-time offender) governs residents held in the system — a visitor meets it only through arrest and detention, which the criminalisation of same-sex conduct makes a live prospect for trans visitors perceived as same-sex-active.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Terrorism, kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Prison axis: no national law, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in any source in this record; the biography of the public figure does not record which section she was assigned to, the October 2024 panel finding concerns the lawfulness of a placement rather than a housing standard, and the report on the proposed cross-dressing ban could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so that bill's status rests on its written summary.
blindSourceSummaries: An August 2024 news report: the beaten body of a transgender social-media personality was found on a highway hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and ordered an investigation — a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

A February 2025 report: six months after the killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; the country has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the 2014 prohibition law reinforced historic-era criminalisation — impunity documented.

An August 2026 report of a foreign government's travel advisory office: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under religious law in 12 state/province.

A March 2025 report: police abuse of people perceived as gay under a law described by those affected as 'weaponised', including a man struck in the mouth with a police weapon and freed only after paying almost half of the bribe demanded for 'looking gay'.

An August 2024 report marking a decade of the prohibition law: the law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; people report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed.
An April 2024 report: luring gangs attract LGBTQ+ people via dating and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

A June 2025 official assessment: same-sex conduct between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; religious law in 12 state/province criminalises same-sex acts, with male same-sex activity carrying the death penalty.

An October 2016 human-rights report: the prohibition law reaches far beyond marriage — it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of same-sex amorous relationship, and gay organisations, with punishments of 10-14 years' prison; documents police torture and arbitrary arrests under it.

An encyclopedic biography of the country's most prominent transgender woman documents the only trans-imprisonment case: pleaded guilty on 5 April 2024, sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, served the term in a maximum-security facility, released on 5 August 2024; press coverage at sentencing openly asked which section she would be kept in, reflecting discretionary placement, and the biography does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section; an October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that the maximum-security placement violated the national correctional-service statute because she was a first-time offender.
A report not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying piece covers transgender people fearing proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.
